---
title: "1.4 — Soundness: why the rules preserve truth"
---

> **Where you are.** A derivation is a tree made from our rules. We now prove that each such
> tree respects Boolean semantics. This concerns our explicitly defined logic, including its
> classical rule, and will justify both the initial search and the final solver.

## 1. The question: what does a derivation guarantee?

A derivation under assumptions doesn't assert an unconditional truth. From the assumption a,
we may derive a, even when a evaluates to false. The guarantee is conditional: every valuation
making all assumptions true must make the conclusion true.


```lean
import Principia.NatDed.Soundness
open Principia Principia.Form
open scoped Principia.Form Principia
```


```text
soundness (d : Γ ⊢ a) : Entails Γ a
Entails Γ a = ∀ v, (∀ b ∈ Γ, eval v b = true) → eval v a = true
```

With no assumptions, every valuation satisfies the empty context. A closed derivation therefore
certifies a tautology. The exercises establish the general result and this corollary.

## 2. Helpers: move between Boolean values and logical evidence

The supplied helper `eval_and v a b` states:

```text
eval v (a ⋏ b) = true ↔ (eval v a = true ∧ eval v b = true)
```

The expression on each side of `↔` is a Lean proposition. On the left, `⋏` builds formula
data; on the right, `∧` pairs two claims about Boolean computations. Here is how to **use** it:

```lean
example (v : Nat → Bool) (a b : Form)
    (h : eval v (a ⋏ b) = true) : eval v b = true := by
  have hparts : eval v a = true ∧ eval v b = true :=
    (eval_and v a b).mp h
  exact hparts.2
```

`.mp` uses the forward direction of an equivalence. `.mpr` uses its reverse direction:

```lean
example (v : Nat → Bool) (a b : Form)
    (ha : eval v a = true) (hb : eval v b = true) :
    eval v (a ⋏ b) = true := by
  exact (eval_and v a b).mpr ⟨ha, hb⟩
```

The supplied `eval_imp` and `eval_or` similarly translate an implication or disjunction's
Boolean truth into Lean evidence about its parts. This lets later proofs focus on rules
rather than repeatedly expanding truth tables.

## 3. Why the induction is on the derivation

We want a guarantee for every allowed proof tree. The final constructor tells us the last
rule used. Induction on that tree gives a guarantee for each smaller premise derivation.
Induction on the formula alone wouldn't tell us which rule was used to prove it.

For conjunction introduction, for example, the two smaller trees derive a and b. Their
induction hypotheses provide truth of a and truth of b whenever Γ is satisfied. `eval_and`
then combines them into truth of the conjunction. For conjunction elimination, one smaller
tree derives a conjunction, and the helper lets us extract the selected component.

This paragraph explains the semantic obligation; the complete induction code is reserved for
the corrections after the exercises. In each branch, read the types of the induction hypotheses
before applying them. They quantify over valuations and satisfied contexts.

### Extending a satisfied context

Rules such as implication introduction add an assumption in a premise. The supplied helper
`sat_cons` extends the corresponding semantic evidence. Its type is:

```text
sat_cons (ha : eval v a = true)
         (hΓ : ∀ b ∈ Γ, eval v b = true) :
  ∀ b ∈ a :: Γ, eval v b = true
```

If Γ is `[c]`, the new context is `[a, c]`. To show every member is true, the helper uses
`ha` for the new head a and `hΓ` for the old tail. Here is a concrete application:

```lean
example (v : Nat → Bool) (a c : Form)
    (ha : eval v a = true) (hc : eval v c = true) :
    ∀ b ∈ [a, c], eval v b = true := by
  have htail : ∀ b ∈ [c], eval v b = true := by
    intro b hb
    simp only [List.mem_singleton] at hb
    subst b
    exact hc
  exact sat_cons ha htail
```

The helper is about truth under one fixed valuation. It doesn't construct a derivation.

### The classical rule still has a Boolean soundness proof

`byContra_eval` says that if truth of `∼a` would force `fls` to evaluate to true, then a
evaluates to true. Check its two possible values: if a is true, the conclusion holds; if a
is false, its negation is true and the premise would imply `false = true`, an impossibility.
This is a finite Boolean argument. Although it validates our system's classical `raa` rule,
it doesn't require Lean's classical excluded-middle principle for arbitrary propositions.

## 4. Read the induction hypotheses as functions

In the conjunction-introduction branch, the proof state has this shape:

```text
da : Γ ⊢ a
db : Γ ⊢ b
iha : Entails Γ a
ihb : Entails Γ b
⊢ Entails Γ (a ⋏ b)
```

The derivations da and db are smaller trees. The induction hypotheses iha and ihb are
semantic guarantees about those trees. After introducing a valuation v and evidence hΓ
that its assumptions hold, `iha v hΓ` has type `eval v a = true`, and `ihb v hΓ` has type
`eval v b = true`. The semantic conjunction helper can combine those pieces.

For implication introduction, the premise's context is a :: Γ. Its induction hypothesis
expects truth of that **extended** context. Supplying only truth of Γ would have the wrong
type; this is why `sat_cons` is needed after introducing evidence that a is true.

For disjunction elimination, there are three premise trees and three induction hypotheses.
One guarantees the disjunction; the other two guarantee the conclusion under their respective
extra assumptions. The Boolean “or” determines which semantic branch to use. The same
conclusion must be established in either case.

## 5. Why the empty context is always satisfied

Context satisfaction asks for truth of every formula in a list. For the empty list there
is no member to inspect. A small example isolates the impossible membership case:

```lean
example (a : Form) (h : a ∈ ([] : List Form)) : False := by
  cases h
```

`List.Mem` has constructors for membership in a nonempty list; none can produce membership
in `[]`. `cases h` therefore leaves no branches. When proving a claim about every member
of the empty context, this same elimination handles the hypothetical member. We still
must introduce the valuation: an empty context doesn't make the formula's value independent
of its valuation; it makes the context's satisfaction condition automatic.

## 7. Hints

**`soundness`.** Induct on the derivation, not the formula. In each branch introduce a valuation and evidence that the context is satisfied. Use the matching semantic helper on goals or hypotheses, and `sat_cons` where a rule extends the context.

**`tautology_of_proof`.** Introduce a valuation, apply soundness, and show every member of the empty context is true. There are no such members: eliminate the impossible membership evidence with `cases`.

## 8. Worked corrections to the required exercises

Try the exercises first. These proofs match `Solution.lean`, checked by `make test`.

### `soundness`

```lean
theorem soundness {Γ : List Form} {φ : Form} (d : Γ ⊢ φ) : Entails Γ φ := by
  induction d with
  | ax h =>
    intro v hΓ
    exact hΓ _ h
  | impI d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    rw [eval_imp]
    intro ha
    exact ih v (sat_cons ha hΓ)
  | impE d1 d2 ih1 ih2 =>
    intro v hΓ
    have hf := ih1 v hΓ
    rw [eval_imp] at hf
    exact hf (ih2 v hΓ)
  | andI d1 d2 ih1 ih2 =>
    intro v hΓ
    rw [eval_and]
    exact ⟨ih1 v hΓ, ih2 v hΓ⟩
  | andE₁ d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    have h := ih v hΓ
    rw [eval_and] at h
    exact h.1
  | andE₂ d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    have h := ih v hΓ
    rw [eval_and] at h
    exact h.2
  | orI₁ d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    rw [eval_or]
    exact Or.inl (ih v hΓ)
  | orI₂ d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    rw [eval_or]
    exact Or.inr (ih v hΓ)
  | orE dor dl dr ihor ihl ihr =>
    intro v hΓ
    have hor := ihor v hΓ
    rw [eval_or] at hor
    cases hor with
    | inl ha => exact ihl v (sat_cons ha hΓ)
    | inr hb => exact ihr v (sat_cons hb hΓ)
  | flsE d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    have h := ih v hΓ
    simp [eval] at h
  | raa d ih =>
    intro v hΓ
    apply byContra_eval
    intro hna
    exact ih v (sat_cons hna hΓ)
```

Each induction hypothesis is an entailment for a premise derivation. The code specializes it to the current valuation and context evidence. Introduction rules build semantic evidence; elimination rules use it. `orE` dispatches the appropriate extended context. The Boolean helper validates `raa` without invoking arbitrary-proposition excluded middle in Lean.

### `tautology_of_proof`

```lean
theorem tautology_of_proof {φ : Form} (d : [] ⊢ φ) : Tautology φ :=
  fun v => soundness d v (by intro ψ h; cases h)
```

An empty list has no members. The function supplied to soundness proves context satisfaction by eliminating impossible membership, leaving validity under the arbitrary valuation.

## 10. Worked corrections to the optional exercises

### `consistency`

```lean
theorem consistency : ([] ⊢ Form.fls) → False := by
  intro d
  have h := tautology_of_proof d (fun _ => false)
  simp [eval] at h
```

A hypothetical closed derivation of falsehood would imply that falsehood evaluates to true under every valuation. Specialize to the all-false valuation. Evaluation gives false, so h is the impossible equality `false = true`, eliminated by simplification.


### `not_provable_var`

```lean
theorem not_provable_var : ([] ⊢ Form.var 0) → False := by
  intro d
  have h := tautology_of_proof d (fun _ => false)
  simp [eval] at h
```

A hypothetical closed derivation of atom 0 would likewise make that atom true under every valuation. The all-false valuation refutes it. Here soundness converts one counterexample into a guarantee that no derivation exists.


## 11. Conclusion

Soundness relates derivation data to semantic truth under satisfied assumptions. Induction
follows the derivation tree because its constructors determine the last rule used. For closed
derivations, context satisfaction is automatic. This theorem will justify a returned certificate
regardless of which search strategy built it; it does not say a search will find every proof.
